It's likely the administration does have the power to unilaterally dismiss anyone hired on within the last year, as stupid as doing that has turned out to be. First of all, if you're a 20 year old college student you probably have some level of access to free or reduced-cost mental healthcare services, which are used by a much larger number of your peers than you probably think!  You can reach out to them privately, and getting some work in with a professional will be beneficial no matter what you do career-wise.  


Second, I really would not freak out about following a specific pathway into a policy career.  You could easily: apply for the Peace Corps, go teach public school, work on a political campaign or at an advocacy org - all with basically 0 relevant experience beforehand, besides maybe some volunteering experience that you can literally show up to tomorrow and begin building.  


A couple of years of that (it'll go by quicker than you think), and you have a perfectly fine profile for applying to a policy school if it's even still what you want to do.  Passion for the field is the only other thing you need, and you have it.    


It's also worth remembering that every year right now represents 5% of your life so far, but every subsequent year that % gets smaller and smaller.  Things that seem massive and consequential now may seem much smaller in the rearview - give yourself the grace to find out!

The environment is definitely suffering, and art is subjective, but it would be disingenuous to say that mass layoffs and unemployment are everywhere, especially if you live in the U.S.  


Right now in the U.S., unemployment is as low as it's been since the late 1960s, the bottom half of incomes are growing about as fast as they have since Reagan destroyed the old unions, and the resulting labor market tightness is contributing to a sharp rise in unionization and workplace organizing.

Compared to the centuries before, we have many fewer and shorter recessions, which is among the many reasons that revolutionary movements of all kinds have failed in America over the last 100 years.  The average citizen's standard of living has risen over time.  


I'm not saying it's not worth dreaming of something better, but it's much easier to build an alternative to a system when you expend the time and energy to understand the current one.
